# Lab 7 — The Characteristic Curves

**Scenario:** `fp-07-characteristic-curves` · five runs of ~12 minutes
(the sweep) · runnable any time after Lab 3

::: {.callout-tip}
## Hands you'll need
Nothing, to run the reference sweep — the gates are scripted. To add
your own points (the assignment), the full circuit kit: Practice Range
drills `d5_enable_condition` and `d6_combinator_pair`.
:::

The Accounting of Flow interlude committed to two formulas and drew
them as a picture: $\mathrm{TH}_{\text{best}}(w) = \min(w/T_0,\, r_b)$
and $\mathrm{CT}_{\text{best}}(w) = \max(T_0,\, w/r_b)$, with the knee
at the critical WIP $W_0 = r_b T_0$. Labs 3 through 6 visited single
points on those curves. This lab buys the whole curve: the same line as
Lab 3, a WIP cap you can set to any level, and one run per level. At the
end you will have drawn the signature figure of *Factory Physics* from
your own measured data — and found the knee.

## The instrument: a ledger made of wire

Capping system WIP requires *knowing* system WIP, live, in-game. The
gate does it the only honest way — the same way FISL does:

1. a **tap belt** just inside the source reads admissions as pulses;
2. a tap belt just before the sink reads completions as pulses;
3. two arithmetic combinators sign them (+1, −1) onto one signal `W`;
4. a self-looped decider accumulates the difference — a memory cell
   whose running value **is** admissions − completions = WIP;
5. the source inserter is enabled only while `W < w`.

You are rebuilding Lab 0's conservation ledger out of combinators, and
the run's census will agree with your wire — the rare lab where the
learner's contraption and the laboratory's instrument are the same
object. (The completion pulses travel home along the line's own belts as
a relay chain, read-disabled, every hop checked: the 9-tile wire-reach
lesson from Lab 3, institutionalized.) This CONWIP mechanism — a
constant WIP cap enforced at admission — is the control policy Hopp &
Spearman's ch. 10 builds its case around; here it is five entities.

## The sweep

Four reference gates plus the ungated baseline:

```sh
fisl solutions scenarios/factory-physics/fp07-characteristic-curves --run \
    --json course/data/lab-07-comparison.json
```

Before running it, fill in this table from the interlude's formulas —
the line is Lab 3's: $r_b = 15/\text{min}$ (the 4 s first machine), and
$T_0 \approx 56$ s if you count the belt ride (walk it and check):

| run | cap $w$ | predicted TH | predicted CT |
|---|---|---|---|
| w-04 | 4 | $\approx$ 4.3/min | $\approx T_0$ |
| w-08 | 8 | $\approx$ 8.6/min | $\approx T_0$ |
| w-14 | 14 $\approx W_0$ | approaching 15/min | near $T_0$ — the knee |
| w-24 | 24 | 15/min | $\approx$ 96 s |
| baseline | uncapped | 15/min | $\approx$ 207 s (Lab 3's number) |

Then plot the measured points: **TH against measured average WIP** and
**CT against measured average WIP**. Two honesty rules make the plot
meaningful:

- The x-coordinate is the *measured* average WIP, never the nominal cap
  — the gate's timing slack and belt discreteness make them differ, and
  the report's number is the true one.
- Expect measured points **at or below** the best-case TH curve (and at
  or above the CT curve). The formulas are bounds; belts and inserter
  swings are real mechanisms. The gap between your points and the bound
  is itself data — where does it come from?

## The measured sweep

| run | measured avg WIP | TH | CT | pooled productive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| w-04 | 4.02 | 5.60/min | **43.02 s** | 24.6% |
| w-08 | 8.03 | 10.90/min | 44.20 s | 48.8% |
| w-14 | 14.04 | **15.00/min** | 56.17 s | 66.9% |
| w-24 | 24.04 | 15.00/min | 96.17 s | 66.9% |
| baseline | 51.70 | 15.00/min | 206.78 s | 66.9% |

![The measured points against the deterministic best case computed from
the *measured* $T_0$. The left branch rides the bound; the flat branch
is Little's Law exactly; the knee sits between the second and third
points.](../images/labs/lab-07-curves.svg){width=100%}

Read the table the way the lab's own rules demand, and it corrects its
authors first: the pre-run prediction table used the walk-estimate
$T_0 \approx 56$ s — and the w-04 run, whose entire job is to measure
$T_0$ directly, came back with **43.02 s**. The belt ride is faster than
the walk suggested; the *estimate* was wrong and the *method* caught it.
With the measured $T_0$: $W_0 = r_b T_0 = 0.25 \times 43.02 \approx
\mathbf{10.8}$ — which the sweep confirms from both sides: w-08 (WIP
8.03) is still on the rising branch at 10.90/min, w-14 already sits at
the full 15.00/min. Everything else lands where the formulas point:

- **The flat branch is Little's Law to the decimal**: CT $= w/r_b = 4w$
  seconds — 56.17 at WIP 14.04, 96.17 at 24.04, 206.78 at 51.70.
- **The left branch rides the bound**: w-04's throughput is
  $4.02/43.02 \times 60 = 5.61$/min against 5.60 measured; w-08 gives
  back ~2.5% to belt discreteness as the line approaches the knee — the
  only visible mechanism gap in the whole sweep.
- **The state fractions are rate ratios**: at 5.60/min, pooled
  productive should be $(5.6/15 + 5.6/30 + 5.6/30)/3 = 24.8\%$;
  measured, 24.6%.
- **Boundaries matter, recursively**: the gate capped its circuit ledger
  at $W < 4$, yet FISL reports average WIP 4.02. No contradiction — the
  tap belts sit one tile *inside* FISL's ports, so the two ledgers
  declare different boundaries and disagree by exactly the material in
  between. Lab 0's first lesson, found again inside your own
  instrument.

## The assignment

The reference sweep leaves the knee bracketed but not pinned: somewhere
in (8, 14], predicted 10.8. Pick caps we didn't run — 10, 11, 12 —
build your own gate (the toolbox holds a full counter kit; the solution
scripts are readable blueprints), and pin it. Two questions to answer
with your additions:

1. **Where exactly is the knee?** Find the smallest cap that still
   yields 15.00/min, and compare with $r_b T_0 = 10.8$ computed from
   w-04's measured $T_0$. If they disagree, one of your boundaries is
   talking — find which.
2. **What does the flat region cost?** Every point right of the knee has
   the same throughput; read the CT column as the price tag of the
   inventory. The measured flat branch already obeys CT $= 4w$ exactly —
   your new points must too, or something is wrong with your gate.

## Debrief

- The machine-state fractions tell the low-WIP story: at $w = 4$, which
  machines are starved and how much? The constraint's idle time left of
  the knee is the *only* throughput cost in this whole deterministic
  world — name the mechanism.
- Your gate held WIP constant; Lab 3's gate held one buffer constant.
  Both landed on the flat region. What does CONWIP's *system-level* cap
  give you that the local gate didn't? (Hint: what happens to each if a
  middle machine slows down for a minute?)
- The curves you drew are the deterministic **best case**. Hopp &
  Spearman's ch. 7 draws two more on the same axes: the worst case and
  the practical worst case. Both need variability to mean anything —
  which is precisely where this course's sequel begins. Your knee at
  $W_0$ is the last thing determinism can teach: with variability,
  operating *at* the knee starves the bottleneck whenever anything
  wobbles, and the whole art becomes how far right of it to sit.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Instructor notes

- All numbers measured (reference dataset in
  `course/data/lab-07-comparison.json`, five runs ~60 min wall time).
  The chapter deliberately keeps the falsified pre-run estimate
  ($T_0 \approx 56$ s from the walk) next to the measured 43.02 s — the
  correction *is* the pedagogy: predictions written down, checked, and
  amended in public. Teach it, don't sand it off.
- The measured cap offset runs +0.02–0.04 *above* the nominal cap, not
  below: the tap belts sit one tile inside FISL's port boundary, so the
  circuit ledger undercounts FISL's WIP by the in-flight material
  between the boundaries (~1 unit at the source side). The chapter's
  "boundaries matter, recursively" bullet is the discussion anchor.
- Expected learner knee-pinning result: smallest full-throughput cap
  between 11 and 12 (predicted $W_0 = 10.8$, integer caps, +1 boundary
  offset — the disagreement-resolution in assignment Q1 is intended,
  not a trap).
- The census cross-check doubles as the meta-lesson: the learner's
  combinator ledger and FISL's conservation ledger count the same
  quantity up to their declared boundaries; if a learner's own gate
  misbehaves, comparing their `W` signal against the panel's live WIP
  is the debugging exercise.
:::
